question: Did God kill all the Egyptian cattle in the sixth plague?
summary: Exodus 9:3-6 (the fifth plague, the murrain — the question's "sixth" is wrong) says "all the cattle of Egypt died." Three verses later at Exodus 9:19, God is warning Egyptians to bring their cattle and servants indoors because hail is coming and what's left in the field will die. So either "all" didn't mean all, or there's a narrative continuity problem between the fifth and seventh plagues.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read "all" as a Hebrew idiom for the bulk of the field-herds, pointing to 9:19 itself as proof that some cattle plainly survived.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the plain wording: if 9:6 says all Egypt's cattle died, then the cattle that 9:19 warns Egyptians to shelter from the hail should not be there to die again.

pd_work.note: Haley treats the 'all the cattle of Egypt died' (Ex. 9:6) vs. surviving cattle (Ex. 9:19) case directly, arguing 'all' is used in a limited, popular sense and the murrain was restricted to cattle in the field.

excerpts.excerpt_text: all the cattle of Egypt died—not absolutely every beast, for we find (Exo 9:19, Exo 9:21) that there were still some left; but a great many died of each herd—the mortality was frequent and widespread.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly names the 9:6 'all died' wording and resolves it against 9:19/9:21, the exact verses in tension; strongest single reconcile because it cites 9:19 explicitly.
